articles.title: Sexual violence can hide in plain sight at music festivals, according to new study
articles.dek: The pressure to maintain an atmosphere of fun and escapism can make it harder for festival organizations to acknowledge and respond to harm, while frontline workers are left…
paragraphs: The pressure to maintain an atmosphere of fun and escapism can make it harder for festival organizations to acknowledge and respond to harm, while frontline workers are left dealing with its consequences, a new study finds.
Previous research into gender-based violence (GBV) at music festivals has largely focused on the experiences of audiences and the risks they face.

A new study from the University of Portsmouth takes a different perspective, examining the experiences of the workers who keep festivals running and are often the first to encounter or respond to violence and harassment. The work is published in the journal Organization .

The research suggests that the atmosphere festivals work to create can make GBV harder to acknowledge. In spaces designed around joy, freedom and escapism, violence can seem out of place or be treated as incompatible with the experience organizers want to promote.
At the same time, organizational politics, workplace hierarchies and unclear processes can combine to make incidents difficult to recognize, understand and act upon.

Based on 24 trauma-informed interviews with festival workers and fieldwork at five U. K. music festivals, the study explores how violence can become part of the background of an event rather than something an organization properly acknowledges and addresses.

One example involved a lighting technician who was asked by a promoter to reduce lighting because it was "ruining the vibe." The technician challenged the decision, saying: "Unless the vibe you're going for is a rapey one, then you need more lighting." The promoter had the final say and kept the lighting low.
This example illustrates how a decision that could improve people's safety can be overridden by the desire to preserve the festival atmosphere.

The study also found that workers could be reluctant to report harassment because of the insecure nature of festival employment. Two women who experienced sexual harassment from a male security guard asked only for him to be told to leave them alone, fearing that making a formal complaint could affect their chances of being employed at future events.

The researchers found that even when incidents were reported, responsibility for dealing with them was often unclear. Disclosures could be redirected, minimized or lost as they passed between teams, while the people receiving them did not always have the authority or support to take action.

In one interview, a worker recalls having encountered four incidents of sexual violence by 10 p. m. at a festival. After briefly retreating to a tent to cry, they returned to their shift while the event continued around them.

The researchers describe this as "organizational disorientation"—a situation in which the atmosphere, working practices and structures of a festival make gender-based violence difficult to recognize, interpret and respond to.

They suggest their findings challenge the idea that the festival atmosphere is simply a backdrop to incidents of violence. Instead, the way festivals are organized, including their informal hierarchies, working practices and competing priorities, can shape whether harm is recognized and addressed.

articles.title: Seafloor clay reveals past dramatic ice loss in West Antarctica
articles.dek: Scientists have discovered the best evidence yet to show that West Antarctica's most vulnerable ice streams—including its giant Thwaites Glacier—repeatedly collapsed and…
paragraphs: Scientists have discovered the best evidence yet to show that West Antarctica's most vulnerable ice streams—including its giant Thwaites Glacier—repeatedly collapsed and retreated far inland during natural warm periods of the last 800,000 years.

The study, published in Nature Communications , suggests much of the region's marine-based ice sheet has a historic "tipping point" triggered by global warming to temperatures similar to those the Earth is experiencing today.

The question of how the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) responded to previous warm periods—known as interglacials—has long divided researchers. Now, an international team led by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) has found the answer buried in mud cores drilled from the nearby ocean floor.

It's a distinctive mineral called kaolinite—what most people know as china clay. It typically forms in warm, wet, tropical climates or swampy environments—like those that existed on the Antarctic continent more than 34 million years ago.

Today, this ancient kaolinite is locked away in the bedrock beneath the WAIS, and it takes the immense weight of glaciers such as Thwaites and neighboring Pine Island to grind it out and carry it offshore in icebergs and water currents.

But sediment cores pulled from 4,000m (13,000 feet) below the sea surface on Antarctica's continental margin tell a dramatic story: During every single interglacial over the past 800,000 years, that kaolinite signal plummeted to near zero.

"When the kaolinite signal at our drill-core sites suddenly collapses, it tells us the marine-based ice in the Amundsen Sea sector of the West Antarctic—including Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers—must have melted and retreated far back into the continent's interior," says Dr. Claus-Dieter Hillenbrand, the BAS marine geologist who led the study.
"It's the only way to explain why the delivery of kaolinite-rich debris to the ocean floor stops."
Identifying that the ice retreated is only half the story, however, so the team wanted to find the cause as well.

They discovered it in a second clay mineral: smectite. Unlike the local clays weathered from Antarctica's own rocks and volcanoes, this specific, magnesium-rich variety carries a chemical signature unique to the deep Pacific Ocean floor far to the north.
Something had to carry the smectite south and deposit it in the nearshore muds—and, crucially, at the same time as the kaolinite disappears.

The obvious explanation is warm deep-water currents intruding onto the West Antarctic continental shelf. These would have transported the smectite south toward the continent, simultaneously melting the grounded ice whose erosion produces the kaolinite signal.

To cement this narrative, the team then turned to the fossilized remains of diatoms—microscopic marine algae—in the mud layers. The shell-like structures take different shapes depending on water temperature.

The results of this analysis revealed a powerful regional thermal amplification. While global average temperatures during past warm periods were only 1. 0°C to 1. 5°C warmer than preindustrial levels (i. e. , similar to today) or even colder, the local waters in front of the WAIS surged to between about 1°C and 3°C warmer than today's near-freezing baseline.

articles.title: Swordfish may be using deep dives to navigate the open ocean
articles.dek: Swordfish spend much of their time hunting prey about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface in the ocean twilight zone, but occasionally, they reach depths of more than…
paragraphs: Swordfish spend much of their time hunting prey about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface in the ocean twilight zone, but occasionally, they reach depths of more than 1,000 meters (3,280 feet). Now, scientists from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) are investigating what may be behind these extreme dives.

The new study , published in Marine Biology , suggests these rare, extreme dives may help swordfish gather information about their surroundings in the open ocean. By moving through different water masses and ocean features, the fish may be sampling changes in ocean conditions for cues that help them navigate during their long-distance movements. The swordfish in the study traveled thousands of miles during their migrations, moving between waters off Canada and the Caribbean.

"If we want to understand how these animals move and navigate to make use of the information in their environment, these rare behaviors can be really valuable," said Martin Arostegui, a marine biologist at WHOI and an author of the study. "Being able to start to get at that question represents just how much more we know about what happens above the surface of the ocean than what we do under it."

During the 3,666 deployment days, "extreme" dives were identified 39 times. This data was collected in partnership with NOAA's Southeast Fisheries Science Center and the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries.

"It wouldn't have been possible to analyze this from just a single tagging operation, or from a single lab," said Simon Thorrold, a fish ecologist at WHOI and author of the study. "It was necessary to pull tagging data from different studies and to begin building longer-term data sets to give us enough power to at least begin to sort of ask questions about what those dives might be for."

"This study demonstrates the value of collaboration and long-term data collection," said Eric Orbesen, a research fishery biologist at the Southeast Fisheries Science Center and co-author on the study. "Individual tagging projects provide important snapshots in time and space, but maintaining and combining these data sets over many years allows scientists to identify behaviors and patterns that would otherwise be very difficult to see."

Understanding how swordfish respond to ocean conditions could also help scientists better predict how these important predators may move as the ocean changes. Swordfish support valuable fisheries and play an important role in marine food webs, making it important to understand where they travel, what influences their movements and how they interact with the changing ocean.

"They could be coming into an ocean weather system, like an eddy or a frontal system, where we have a change in water masses. Maybe that change in the ocean system prompts them to check out what's happening deeper in the water column—to get a sense of where they are, how deep the feature extends or answer other questions about their world that we don't even know they're asking yet," said Ciara Willis, who led the study as a doctoral student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program. Willis is now a postdoctoral investigator at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute.

Researchers still don't know to what extent extreme diving is shared broadly across swordfish or how it varies among populations or life stages. They also want to determine how important these rare dives are to swordfish overall and whether they represent an occasional way of gathering information or a more significant part of how these highly migratory predators navigate the ocean.

articles.title: AI-generated molecular fingerprints help identify existing compounds with therapeutic potential
articles.dek: Health care researchers have long sought to harness the power of computing to design molecules that bind to specific receptors and can be used as targeted treatments for…
paragraphs: Health care researchers have long sought to harness the power of computing to design molecules that bind to specific receptors and can be used as targeted treatments for diseases. Even with the increasing sophistication of artificial intelligence, however, this technological promise has yet to be realized.
Junmei Wang, professor of pharmaceutical sciences in the School of Pharmacy, is tackling the problem from a different perspective.

In a paper published Oct. 28 in the journal Science Advances , Wang outlined Full-Spectrum Generative Lead Discovery (FSGLD), a novel, practical and reusable framework that takes advantage of generative AI to screen for existing compounds with potential for therapeutic development.

Developing pharmaceuticals using AI isn't new, but it is laborious and often leads to a dead end. "If you generate a brand-new molecule, that's actually a limitation," Wang said. "A lot of compounds can't be synthesized, and that is a big issue."

"We use a simpler representation of a molecule: a molecular fingerprint," Wang said, referring to a digital encoding of a molecule's key chemical features. To uncover patterns in the fingerprints that might point to useful properties, Wang's lab used a generative adversarial network called DRUG-GAN. This system is made of two components: a generator that creates fake fingerprints and a discriminator that attempts to distinguish the fakes from fingerprints of real molecules.

This back-and-forth is the GAN's training. Over time, the generator learns to generate fingerprints that more closely resemble those of real molecules. Researchers then search chemical databases for existing compounds with similar fingerprints; the AI-generated pattern leads to the discovery of real molecules that researchers can test—no need to synthesize a new molecule.
In this work, the lab screened for target-specific compounds, or molecules that bind to and act on a receptor related to a particular disease or condition.
They screened for compounds linked to two of the most commonly targeted drug receptors: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and protein kinase.
"We saw good results," Wang said. The team identified novel compounds that were different from the molecules used to train the GAN, but that would still bind to the target receptors.
The promise of FSGLD goes beyond these two receptors; much of its value lies in its flexibility.
"It's a reusable framework that connects generative AI with practical compound discovery."

Wang's lab is taking advantage of this flexibility to explore two complementary approaches. One, called ADSeqGAN, generates new molecular structures by learning from text-based descriptions of molecules, without requiring a receptor's three-dimensional structure. Another, currently in development and called DRUG-FF, uses the three-dimensional shape of a receptor and/or a bound molecule to guide the design of new compounds that could fit the binding site.

articles.title: Pa. Gov. Josh Shapiro’s popularity and ‘get sh-t done’ attitude might not cut it in crowded 2028 Democratic field – but he has options
articles.dek: The 2026 midterm elections swept Democrats into office around the country in such numbers that journalists were running out of synonyms for “ massive .”
paragraphs: The 2026 midterm elections swept Democrats into office around the country in such numbers that journalists were running out of synonyms for “ massive .”

In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection by 22 percentage points, winning more than 60% of the vote – something that has been accomplished only twice before in the modern era in the Keystone State.

Not only did Shapiro wipe the floor with his opponent Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer, but he also helped flip four U. S. House seats from red to blue. His coattails benefited down-ballot candidates , helping Democrats solidify their control of the state House and flip the state Senate as well .
Shapiro’s political stock in Pennsylvania is riding high.

I’m a political science professor and political media researcher in central Pennsylvania, and many of my former students work in Harrisburg. Some are Democrats working for or around the governor; others are Republicans working in different corners of state government. All are finely tuned to the political gossip that swirls around a successful politician whose star is on the rise. It is the worst-kept secret in American politics that Josh Shapiro wants to be president.

I’ve met the governor a handful of times and can attest to his George Clooney-level charisma. He’s a hard worker, has maintained a remarkably clean political profile, and is from many accounts a genuinely nice dude.
And yet, there are plenty of reasons his ambitions may require some careful timing, regardless of his personal strengths.

Shapiro’s political victories didn’t just happen. Over the past four years, he has worked to demonstrate bipartisan competence as Pennsylvania’s chief executive, adopting an expression he uses frequently: “ get sh-t done .”
Now, with Democrats holding the governor’s office and both chambers of the General Assembly, Shapiro told reporters : “We got the power now, the House, the Senate. We have to deliver.”

Shapiro’s approval ratings have remained strong , consistent with his reelection margins. That’s unusual in a state that has swung back and forth between supporting Donald Trump in 2016 , Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024 , each time by fewer than 2 percentage points.
If Shapiro is indeed seriously eyeing the White House , his current popularity will certainly serve him well. But winning the presidency is an enormous undertaking, particularly in a crowded field.

With Trump unable to run in 2028, the next presidential election will feature open seats for both parties and likely attract many candidates. Democrats, in particular, have a deep bench of attractive potential contenders .

There are so many possibilities that Shapiro could find himself running against people very much like him: younger centrists, swing-state politicians and accomplished elected officials with solid records. Consider just a few names that could be part of the conversation: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel.

Shapiro would have to find a way to distinguish himself in a field filled with candidates who can make many of the same arguments about their experience, political appeal and accomplishments. That’s a tall order. A Plan B might be wise.

He could run for the Senate in 2028 against incumbent John Fetterman, if Fetterman seeks reelection . This would be a twofer: Shapiro would continue his rise in politics, and he would likely beat a guy he apparently does not like. The two reportedly don’t speak , much less get along.

Shapiro could also position himself for a vice presidential nomination by attaching himself to another 2028 hopeful. This would buy him time to build his national profile, allow the presidential field to sort itself out and potentially put him in a strong position for another run at the White House down the road. It would also give him an opportunity to demonstrate that he can work effectively on a national stage.

Or he could angle for a Cabinet post. The federal government has undergone significant restructuring under DOGE and Trump’s executive orders. Should a Democrat win the White House in 2028, rebuilding federal agencies and restoring institutional capacity will be a monumental undertaking. Shapiro could be an attractive candidate for a major administrative role.

The bottom line for Shapiro is that he will need to distinguish himself from a crowded field of Democrats by emphasizing his statewide victories in a major swing state, impressive fundraising ability and a political voice that can evoke Barack Obama without alienating either his party or the broader electorate. That’s a tricky feat, even for the most talented politicians.

But Nov. 3, 2026, showed us that he knows how to make sh-t happen. Whatever he decides, the next two years will be important for Shapiro, consequential for Democrats, and fascinating for political scientists like me, who will be watching events unfold with a keen eye and, probably, a bucket of popcorn.

articles.title: Detailed 3D view of babesiosis parasite's ribosome could guide development of targeted treatments
articles.dek: A new study has revealed a three-dimensional, near-atomic-resolution view of the ribosome from Babesia divergens, one of several Babesia species known to infect humans and…
paragraphs: A new study has revealed a three-dimensional, near-atomic-resolution view of the ribosome from Babesia divergens, one of several Babesia species known to infect humans and cause babesiosis. The structural insights from this close-up view could help researchers identify parasite-specific features that may be exploited for future drug development.

The research also deepens the foundations of knowledge for the entire group of protozoa to which Babesia belongs, known as apicomplexan parasites, that are responsible for diseases including malaria and toxoplasmosis. The study is published in Nature Communications .

Very little is known about the fundamental mechanisms that these complex pathogens rely on to cause infection and survive in a diverse range of host species, said Mélissa Léger-Abraham, assistant professor of microbiology in the Blavatnik Institute at Harvard Medical School and HMS assistant professor of pediatrics at Boston Children's Hospital and senior author of the study.

"Having detailed images of the Babesia ribosome lays an important foundation for deepening our understanding of how the organism lives and gives us step-by-step guidance in the search for new drugs to treat babesiosis," Léger-Abraham said.

The researchers focused their studies on the ribosome, which is a large molecule composed of ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) and ribosomal proteins. Ribosomes are cellular biochemical machines that read an organism's genetic sequence and translate it into proteins that the cell needs to survive.

This process, and the ribosome itself, is the target of more than half of the antibiotics currently used against bacterial infections. Therefore, a detailed understanding of the ribosomes of other pathogens, such as parasites, could provide crucial information on how they differ from other organisms like humans or bacteria.

"Once we can see the differences between parasite and human ribosomes, we could design drugs that interrupt the parasite's life cycle and its ability to infect humans, without interfering with any of the processes that our bodies rely on to keep us healthy," Léger-Abraham said.

Babesia divergens is a tick-borne pathogen prevalent in Europe that causes significant livestock loss and sometimes severe disease—even death—in humans, especially people with compromised immune systems. The disease can spread from one human to another in donated blood and from pregnant mothers to their babies. There are many different species of Babesia that cause this disease in humans.

In the United States, cases rose by 9% per year from 2015 to 2022, as the blacklegged ticks that host the closely related Babesia microti have increased their geographic range and the length of their biting season due to warming temperatures.

Léger-Abraham, who has a strong interest in deepening the understanding of neglected tropical diseases, said she was initially interested in imaging ribosomes from Plasmodium, the genus of pathogens that cause malaria, because of its significant global health impact. However, she chose an organism related to Plasmodium, Babesia divergens, because it is easy to cultivate and can produce larger quantities of material required for high-resolution structural studies.

The researchers used cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to image a sample of ribosome particles from Babesia divergens. In cryo-EM, many copies of the particles to be analyzed are rapidly frozen in a thin layer of vitreous ice, which is then imaged, providing two-dimensional views of the particles. Researchers then computationally align and combine the resulting two-dimensional images capturing different orientations of the same particles to reconstruct a three-dimensional model. Data were collected at the Harvard Cryo-EM Center for Structural Biology at HMS.

The structural map Léger-Abraham and colleagues assembled of the Babesia divergens cytosolic ribosomes described the intricate interactions between residues from ribosomal proteins and ribonucleotides from the rRNA. It is the most detailed map of this kind ever generated for an apicomplexan parasite.

Moreover, it is detailed enough to observe chemical modifications of the ribosome that could modulate its function. If you think of RNA as a language, these modifications work like punctuation, accents, and other diacritical marks to subtly modify the meaning of the code.

articles.title: Germany's Isar Aerospace eyes overtaking Elon Musk's SpaceX
articles.dek: The head of Germany's Isar Aerospace voiced hope Tuesday that the company could one day overtake Elon Musk's SpaceX to become the world's premier space launch company.
paragraphs: The head of Germany's Isar Aerospace voiced hope Tuesday that the company could one day overtake Elon Musk's SpaceX to become the world's premier space launch company.
Daniel Metzler, who founded the company with two fellow students in 2018, pointed to a huge backlog of launch orders, helped by European military clients.
"SpaceX was founded in 2002. Back then I was playing with Pokemon cards," he said. "Looking at what could happen in the next 18 years, I wouldn't rule out us being further ahead than SpaceX."
Isar became in September the first privately financed European company to get a rocket into orbit.
Europe is betting that competition between Isar and other players such as Rocket Factory Augsburg will bring down the price of satellite launches.

This would help ensure affordable access to space for sectors ranging from telecommunications to defense, independent of entities such as SpaceX, the sector leader valued at $1. 9 trillion (1. 7 trillion euros).
Speaking at a conference organized by the SZ newspaper, Metzler said Isar had already come a long way, noting that SpaceX needed four attempts to get into orbit compared to Isar's two.
Capacity rather than demand was now the big bottleneck, Metzler added.
He said the company was 15 times oversubscribed for 2028 launches as European governments now preferred European providers to put their defense satellites up as opposed to firms overseas.
"There are 14 customers for every rocket that we have to disappoint," he said.
"About 18 months ago, 85% of inquiries were commercial and 15% were military, and that ratio has since flipped," he added.
Isar is working on developing reusable rockets to boost capacity and bring launch costs down, hoping to catch up with SpaceX's reusable Falcon 9 rocket.
"Already with our next launch, for which we are currently finalizing the launch vehicle, we will be taking initial measurements to assess the reentry of the rocket's first stage," he said.
"Over the next three or four flights, we also plan to start flying hardware specifically designed for reusability."

articles.title: Students creating documentaries with scientists deepens STEM belonging and public trust in science
articles.dek: Marine scientists navigate autonomous glider robots across the Atlantic Ocean and along the West Antarctic Peninsula , collecting data to help predict storm intensity.
paragraphs: Marine scientists navigate autonomous glider robots across the Atlantic Ocean and along the West Antarctic Peninsula , collecting data to help predict storm intensity.
When farmers’ fields are destroyed by an unknown pathogen, plant scientists spend years breeding new varieties of disease-resistant food crops.
A team of microbiologists explore deep-sea volcanoes in search of organisms that may contain anticancer compounds.

These are passionate people who are dedicated to seeking solutions to real-world problems. They are also the main characters in science documentaries produced in the Rutgers Immersive Learning Science Storytelling Lab that I oversee. Our lab pairs students with working scientists to co-create documentaries about research as it happens, while earning experiential learning credit.
At a time when confidence in science is declining , I was approached by scientists who wanted their authentic research stories communicated to broad audiences.

I am an educator, a researcher and anthropologist , and a science filmmaker who has been making science documentaries with Rutgers students and researchers since 2008. The science-in-action storytelling model I developed is intended to make the human journey of science visible to the public. Our stories communicate the process, motivations and integrity behind science, which helps earn public confidence and trust in science .

I also partner with STEM learning researchers to gauge whether our documentaries increase the relatability of scientists, increase public understanding of scientific processes and help students find belonging in STEM.
Science-in-action storytelling is composed of five steps that support student-scientist relationships.
First, the storytellers develop trust with the participating university scientists. This trust stems from shared respect and a mutual understanding of the co-creation process.
The scientists then invite storytellers into their labs and field sites, where we capture their research processes in real time. This is Step 2.

Our professional storytelling team, which includes students, then documents scientists conducting research, including experiments and data collection, as they describe the why and how of their work. Depending on the complexity of the project, we collect dozens to hundreds of hours of science-in-action video footage.

Importantly, this video data is maintained in our storytelling lab, as it often includes recordings of federally funded research. Maintaining the video data repository is a key component to establishing and sustaining trust with the participating scientists.

Step 3 invites students to immerse themselves in the video data and begin shaping the footage into documentary scenes, constructed using only the scientists’ words, without narration. As they analyze hours of footage, our students learn about the authentic scientific processes; in doing so, they participate in research through the process of storytelling.
Our students are not graded on their documentary skills, nor are they required to make a film. Instead, they are graded on the science they learn through the storytelling process.

Step 4 requires that the students share drafts of their documentary scenes with the featured scientist to verify the accuracy of the science communicated. This step is part of the foundational trust agreement with the scientists but is also an opportunity for the students to personally connect with scientists.

For Step 5, our lab works to distribute the documentaries to a wide variety of audiences, including the general public. Here we partner with STEM learning experts to assess audiences’ understanding of and trust in the science communicated in the film and audience perceptions of the featured scientists.

Our completed science-in-action documentaries have reached audiences far beyond the university. Our National Science Foundation-funded “ Antarctic Edge: 70° South ” had a theatrical release and aired on Netflix. “ Atlantic Crossing ” was broadcast on PBS stations and was included in a three-year Smithsonian exhibit . “ Fields of Devotion ” was shared by the Association of American Universities as part of its campaign to increase public trust in science . And our lab’s newest long-form documentary, “ Mysteries of 9° North ,” co-created with 14 undergraduates and featuring scientists studying life at deep-sea volcanoes, will be released to the public in early 2027.

Our surveys capture how these science documentaries change audience understanding of science and how it is done. For example, after screening “ Antarctic Edge ,” viewers’ self-reported understanding of climate change rose from 71% to 91% . On a 15-item knowledge quiz, average scores rose, with gains of up to 24 percentage points on the concepts they knew least about.

When 102 undergraduates were asked what made the scientists in “ Fields of Devotion ” relatable, they named passion for the subject (72%), desire to help others (71%) and commitment to their work (70%).

Our survey results also suggest that students who participated in the lab gained confidence and feelings of belonging in a science community. Undergraduates who once said they did not feel “smart enough” reported that they could now see themselves as scientists . All participating students reported that their collaboration with scientists positively transformed their understanding of science.
Nonscience majors gained a deep understanding of the scientific process, while science majors gained rare access to research outside their own disciplines.

Student-directed science documentaries include “ Growing the Caribbean Glider Fleet ,” featuring scientists monitoring hurricane development; “ Biting Back: The Lifesaving Potential of Catnip ,” about the development of natural insect repellents; “ Where Waters Meet on the Breathing Shore ,” featuring climate scientists studying coastal ecosystems; “ The B. A. S. I. L Project ,” about USDA-funded plant-breeding research; “ Ocean Farming ,” about NOAA supported oyster breeding; “ The Women of Nsongwe ,” about USAID-supported agriculture projects in Zambia; and “ Skycatcher ,” about an NSF-funded atmospheric chemistry study in Alabama.

This science-in-action model offers a path forward that other universities could follow. Institutions can strengthen students’ STEM learning and science identities while training a new generation of credible, relatable voices for science.

articles.title: Democrats’ agenda will be set by their ability to organize and compromise — not by the socialist, progressive or centrist factions all claiming victory
articles.dek: The massive Democratic majority in the U. S. House and Senate that was ushered in by a historic blue midterm vote is an ideologically diverse one .
paragraphs: The massive Democratic majority in the U. S. House and Senate that was ushered in by a historic blue midterm vote is an ideologically diverse one .

Candidates spent much of the past year differentiating their positions from the mainstream Democratic coalition. The result is a freshman class filled with as many progressive liberals as moderate problem solvers .

By the morning after Election Day, pundits and current Democratic members across the political spectrum were quick to claim their ideologically aligned candidates as the “ majority makers ” – the group most responsible for the large victory.
Centrist Democrats pointed to pragmatic moderates flipping Trump-won seats. Liberal voices highlighted the enthusiasm and turnout driven by a new, progressive vision.
As a result, days after the election the focus had turned toward January: Who will become the majority maker within Congress?

Party caucus leaders have already started building their roster : The Progressive Caucus claims at least 25 new members in their ranks, growing their membership to over 100 Democratic members. The moderate Blue Dog Caucus doubled in size , from 10 to 20 new members. And in the middle, the center-left New Dems are projecting a caucus of over 140 members.

I’m a political scientist who has worked in and now studies Congress . Figuring out the dynamics and direction of the 120th Congress requires looking at more than the ideological positions of the candidates who won. Instead, focusing on the number of candidates who won can provide insight into the direction of the party as a whole.

The large – and at the time of writing, still growing – margins of Democratic control in the 120th Congress are the biggest since 1993 , before Congress became consistently competitive and increasingly polarized. Those large margins provide essential context for understanding how this new ideological coalition will work in Congress.

While history demonstrates that an ideologically diverse party can be hard to wrangle , the size of the new Democratic majority provides some breathing room for policy negotiation and procedural debates.

Unlike the current Republican Caucus that is reliant on keeping historically narrow majorities together to pass party goals, future Democratic leadership can stand to lose a few votes. With a minimum of 254 seats in the House and 54 seats in the Senate , small-scale Democratic defections are irrelevant.
This breathing room provides the potential for negotiation, while also limiting any mandate an ideological group may claim.

For instance, the 120th Congress will have eight members in the House who are backed or affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America , known as the DSA. In raw terms of political power, when the majority has at least 36 votes to spare on any given party-line bill, this group may not matter in policymaking.

If a group – say, the entirety of the Progressive Caucus’ 100-plus membership – decides to stick together, leadership will be forced to listen. Thus, the potential power of ideological factions depends not only on their ideas but their own organizational skills.

When groups in Congress develop practices such as confidential meetings or binding rules that require members vote together on certain votes, the legitimacy of group demands can be strengthened. This is a strategy that has been employed with relative success by the far-right Republican Freedom Caucus since it was formed in 2014.
The overarching policy goals for newly elected Democrats are consistent across the ideological spectrum: lowering the cost of living and rooting out corruption.

This was highlighted in acceptance speeches by Democrats from South Carolina to Texas to Michigan . All emphasized the same policy-focused promise: Instead of fighting left versus right, the fight should focus on the top versus the bottom.
This shared vision is no doubt important. My research has shown that a cohesive message is a key part of winning and maintaining majority control.

However, the “blue tsunami” was powered by voters with very specific policy demands. And as is always the case with policymaking, the details matter. Does healthcare reform mean reinstating the Obamacare subsidies set to expire on Jan. 1, 2027? Or does it mean something bolder, such as Medicare for All ?

But the power and success of congressional leadership lies in its procedural acumen, not its ideological vision. Some already in Congress have noted New York Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries’ experience and working relationships in discussions of whether he should be house speaker. Furthermore, groups can extract concessions during leadership selection in exchange for their support, such as seats on powerful committees or an agreement on policy agenda items.

articles.title: Massive Study of 2.8 Million People Reveals New Secrets of Alzheimer’s Disease
articles.dek: A genetic analysis of 2. 8 million people points to specific brain cells that may influence Alzheimer’s, offering researchers new leads to investigate in the search for treatments.
paragraphs: A genetic analysis of 2. 8 million people points to specific brain cells that may influence Alzheimer’s, offering researchers new leads to investigate in the search for treatments.

Alzheimer’s disease is the leading cause of dementia, which is projected to affect more than 150 million people worldwide by 2050. Genes play a substantial role in Alzheimer’s risk, but scientists still do not fully understand which genes matter or how they influence the disease. Connecting those genetic clues to what happens inside the brain could help researchers identify possible targets for treatment.

An international team has now identified 127 regions of human DNA associated with Alzheimer’s risk, including 48 that had not previously been mapped in this context. The findings offer a more detailed view of the biological processes involved, pointing to roles for both the brain’s immune cells and several specific types of nerve cells.

Led by Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and published in Nature , the research is the largest genetic association study of Alzheimer’s to date. Researchers analyzed genetic data from approximately 2. 8 million people with diverse genetic backgrounds, including 183,620 people with Alzheimer’s.

“We already knew that immune processes play an important role in Alzheimer’s disease. What makes this study particularly valuable is that we can now connect new genetic risk factors to more specific biological processes, while also uncovering evidence pointing to the involvement of other brain cell types. This gives us a more detailed picture of the biology underlying Alzheimer’s and provides new directions for investigating potential treatments,” said research lead Danielle Posthuma of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.

The analysis strengthened the evidence for the involvement of microglia, immune cells in the brain that help clear away harmful substances and damaged cellular material. Linking genetic risk factors to the processes these cells carry out gives researchers more specific biological connections to investigate.

For the first time, the researchers also identified several specific types of neurons, the cells that receive and transmit information, that were enriched for genetic signals associated with Alzheimer’s. In other words, the genetic evidence pointed toward these particular cell types more often than expected. The findings suggest that they may play a key role in the disease’s development, opening research directions beyond the immune system.

Pooling data from 30 research groups allowed the team to detect genetic associations that might have gone unnoticed in smaller studies. The collaboration brought together academic researchers, biobanks, and industry under the International Psychiatric Genomics Consortium. Its Alzheimer’s disease working group is co-led by Posthuma and Ole Andreassen of the University of Oslo.

Among the contributors was the University of Exeter-led PROTECT study. Professor Anne Corbett of the University of Exeter, who leads PROTECT, said, “This exciting new genetic analysis has uncovered new information on how our genes influence our risk of Alzheimer’s disease. We’re delighted that the PROTECT-UK study contributed to these important new findings. PROTECT collects genetic samples from all participants through a simple at-home saliva sample. This data can then be combined with cohorts from around the world to help us to better understand dementia risk and how it can be treated.”

The genetic associations provide starting points for further investigation, rather than proof that targeting a particular gene will produce an effective treatment. Follow-up research must establish which associations reflect a causal role in Alzheimer’s and whether intervening in the processes involved would be safe and meaningfully beneficial.

articles.title: An Ancient Virus May Hold the Secret to What Makes the Human Brain Different
articles.dek: Could a virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago help explain how the human brain became different?
paragraphs: Could a virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago help explain how the human brain became different?

Researchers at Lund University have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome silences a gene involved in early human brain development. Their study, published in Science Advances , found that the gene, LINC00662, remains active in human brain organoids, where it helps support the development of nerve cells and the connections between them.

The finding offers a way to explore how humans and chimpanzees developed different biological traits despite sharing much of their genetic makeup. Evolution can change how existing genes are used, as well as which genes a species carries.

“The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is important to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development,” says Johan Jakobsson, professor of molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.

The genetic remnant belongs to PTERV1, an endogenous retrovirus. Its DNA became embedded in the chimpanzee genome during an ancient infection and has been inherited ever since. The researchers found copies of the viral sequence at numerous locations throughout chimpanzee DNA.

Those sequences are systematically shut down through methylation, a chemical process that helps regulate gene activity. At the LINC00662 location, the inherited viral insertion also keeps the neighboring gene silent.

To examine this difference during brain development, the team grew brain organoids from human and chimpanzee stem cells. These miniature, three-dimensional structures resemble brain tissue and reproduce some features of its early development.
“The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids,” says Patricia Gerdes, a postdoctoral researcher in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.
The researchers then tested whether the viral sequence caused the shutdown. Using the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool, they removed it from chimpanzee cells. LINC00662 became active again.
“This shows that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees,” says Patricia Gerdes.

A separate experiment explored the gene’s role in humans. When the team used CRISPR to silence LINC00662 in human brain organoids, genes involved in nerve cell development and the formation of connections between those cells became less active.

For Jakobsson, the results show how an infection can leave a lasting genetic change across a population, while helping explain how gene regulation can protect the brain or contribute to damage. The team will next investigate whether other viral remnants influenced brain evolution and whether such sequences are linked to brain diseases.

articles.title: After midterm rout, Republicans can still confirm a Supreme Court justice, but at what cost?
articles.dek: The 2026 midterm rout that awarded Democrats decisive majorities in the Senate and House has also sparked interest in the future of the U. S. Supreme Court .
paragraphs: The 2026 midterm rout that awarded Democrats decisive majorities in the Senate and House has also sparked interest in the future of the U. S. Supreme Court .

With Democrats securing at least a 54-seat majority in the Senate on Jan. 3, 2027 , the window is rapidly closing for President Donald Trump to appoint a new Supreme Court justice and safeguard conservative dominance on the court for decades.

As a Supreme Court scholar , I know that judicial appointments have real consequences. Look no further than Roe v. Wade : Within two years of securing a 6–3 conservative majority, the high court in 2022 eliminated the constitutional right to abortion that had existed for almost 50 years.
Now that Democrats have taken the Senate, if a Republican-appointed justice retires before Jan. 3, it will trigger one of the most explosive confirmation battles in American history.
Here’s how the fight is likely to play out – and why the stakes are so high.

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas top the list of potential retirees after Democrats won the Senate – even if Alito has reportedly said he will not retire immediately . Alito and Thomas are the court’s oldest justices, at 76 and 78, respectively. Thomas is the court’s longest-serving justice, appointed by President George H. W. Bush in 1991.

Perhaps more importantly, both justices have deep ties to the conservative legal movement . This is a network of lawyers, judges and politicians who seek to etch conservative principles into law. Overturning Roe v. Wade was at the top of the conservative wish list .
My research suggests that both Alito and Thomas care about their legacies . And they both understand that a Democratic-controlled Senate will block another Trump-appointed nominee.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer made this clear just days after the midterms. And in October 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee member Richard Blumenthal, the Democrat from Connecticut , said, “It is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration.”
Though Alito has indicated he intends to stay on the court through its 2026 term, Thomas has made no recent public statements about retirement. And Alito is free to change his mind at any time.

If Alito or Thomas announce their retirement soon, Republicans would have enough time to confirm a successor. The Senate has four and a half work weeks scheduled between Election Day and Jan. 3. Justice Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed less than a month after her nomination, making the timeline tight but doable.

Democrats will likely attempt to slow down the process, but they face an uphill battle with few options. Republicans stripped away key delaying tactics in recent years by ending the filibuster in 2017 and ignoring the Judiciary Committee’s quorum rules in 2020. This rule requires nine members be present to transact business, including two members of the minority party.
A Republican effort to confirm a Supreme Court nominee during a lame-duck Senate would spark a historic battle with Democrats.

Democrats would surely point to how Republicans handled President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland in 2016. A seat on the court opened up after conservative Antonin Scalia died on Feb. 13, almost nine months before the November presidential election.

Republicans refused to move Garland’s nomination through the confirmation process, using their majority power to set the Senate’s agenda . This marked the first time since 1866 that a Supreme Court nomination that was not withdrawn failed to receive an up-or-down vote in the Senate.

To justify this, Republicans created the so-called “ McConnell Rule ,” named after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky. According to McConnell , the Senate should not fill Supreme Court vacancies “in the middle of a presidential election year.”
Four years later, Senate Republicans abruptly abandoned the rule . This allowed them to push through Coney Barrett’s confirmation just days before the 2020 presidential election.
Schumer pulled no punches in a speech the day of Barrett’s confirmation vote. Schumer said the day “will go down as one of the darkest days in the 231-year history of the United States Senate.”

He alleged the Republican majority made “a mockery of its own stated principle – that the American people deserve a voice in the selection of Supreme Court Justices – completing the partisan theft of two seats on the Supreme Court using completely contradictory rationales.”
Democrats were clearly outraged by what they saw as two stolen Supreme Court seats.
However, I believe that pushing through a nominee will trigger an even fiercer fight. Senate Democrats will see such a confirmation as a power grab that sidelines the voice of voters.
Furthermore, if a Republican justice retires after the midterms, the move will almost certainly be viewed as purely partisan.

This has the potential to further erode public support for the court , which is sitting near historic lows . And it will likely fuel the fire of Supreme Court reform, including the possibility of expanding the number of justices on the court .
Put simply, in securing a short-term conservative victory, Republicans may end up handing Democrats the exact justification they need to reshape the high court.

articles.title: NASA to Welcome Expedition 74 Astronauts Home at Space Center Houston
articles.dek: NASA will welcome home the Expedition 74 crew during a public event at Space Center Houston following their return from a long-duration mission aboard the International Space…
paragraphs: NASA will welcome home the Expedition 74 crew during a public event at Space Center Houston following their return from a long-duration mission aboard the International Space Station.

NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, and Chris Williams; ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot; and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud‑Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev will share mission highlights at 6 p. m. CST Tuesday, Nov. 17, at NASA Johnson Space Center’s visitor center. An awards ceremony recognizing key mission contributors will follow the presentation.

The astronauts will be available for media interviews before the event. Media may request an in-person interview no later than 5 p. m. Monday, Nov. 16, by emailing the JSC Newsroom at jsc-newsroom@mail. nasa. gov .

Williams, Kud‑Sverchkov, and Mikaev launched aboard the Soyuz MS-28 spacecraft from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on Nov. 27, 2025. The trio returned to Earth on July 26, making a parachute-assisted landing southeast of Dzhezkazgan, Kazakhstan. The crew was in space for 241 days, orbiting the Earth 3,856 times and traveling more than 102 million miles. The mission was the first for Williams and Mikaev and the second for Kud-Sverchkov.

Meir, Hathaway, and Adenot launched aboard a Dragon spacecraft on Feb. 13 as part of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. After more than seven months aboard the space station, Meir, Hathaway, and Adenot safely splashed down on Oct. 8 in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles.

During their 237-day mission, the four crew members traveled more than 100 million miles and completed more than 3,792 orbits around Earth. The mission was the second for Meir and the first for Hathaway and Adenot. Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev also flew as part of Crew-12 but is unavailable for the event.

The Expedition 74 crew dedicated more than 1,400 hours to scientific research and technology demonstrations aboard the International Space Station. Its work advanced in-space manufacturing by testing metal and tissue 3D-printing technologies and supported human health studies examining the effects of long-duration spaceflight. Research included blood flow studies, assessments of piloting capabilities under changing gravitational conditions, and activation of a new compact exercise system . The crew also evaluated life-support and environmental systems critical to future exploration missions under NASA’s Artemis program.

In addition, the crew members conducted pharmaceutical research to crystalize proteins for cancer medications , advance tumor targeting treatments , and grow stem cells for therapeutics. They cared for the first set of plants studied outside of curated systems , upgraded an instrument used to advance our understanding of matter and develop new quantum technologies, managed visiting spacecraft, and performed essential maintenance to support the continued operation of the orbiting laboratory.

Beyond research and operational achievements, Expedition 74 engaged students and audiences around the world through live educational events, outreach activities, and the sharing of stunning imagery that highlights the importance of scientific discovery and international collaboration in space.

For more than 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs not possible on Earth. The space station helps NASA understand and overcome the challenges of human spaceflight, expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit, and build on the foundation for long-duration missions to the Moon, as part of the Artemis program, and to Mars.

articles.title: James Webb Discovers a Nearly Pristine Galaxy From the Dawn of the Universe
articles.dek: A galaxy seen 13 billion years ago has just 1/240th the Sun’s oxygen abundance, offering a rare glimpse of what the ancestors of the Milky Way’s faintest neighbors may have…
paragraphs: A galaxy seen 13 billion years ago has just 1/240th the Sun’s oxygen abundance, offering a rare glimpse of what the ancestors of the Milky Way’s faintest neighbors may have looked like.

Some of the faintest galaxies near the Milky Way may be survivors from the earliest chapters of cosmic history. Their ancient stars preserve clues about how galaxies formed, but astronomers have struggled to connect these nearby relics to the small, primitive galaxies that existed billions of years ago.

An international research team led by Associate Professor Kimihiko Nakajima of Kanazawa University has now identified a possible link. A tiny galaxy called LAP1-B, seen as it existed 13 billion years ago, contains remarkably little oxygen and has several characteristics that resemble some of the oldest galaxies still found near the Milky Way.

The chemical evidence reaches back to a time when the universe was only beginning to acquire the elements familiar to us today. Shortly after the Big Bang, the universe consisted primarily of hydrogen and helium. Heavier elements, including the carbon and oxygen essential for life, were produced later inside the first generations of stars and eventually released into space.

Astronomers have long wanted to study galaxies from this early period to understand how those elements first accumulated. The challenge is that such galaxies are extraordinarily small and faint, making their chemical composition difficult to measure even with powerful telescopes.

LAP1-B became accessible thanks to gravitational lensing, a phenomenon in which the gravity of a massive object bends and magnifies light from something farther away. In this case, a massive galaxy cluster amplified the distant galaxy’s light approximately 100 times, allowing researchers to examine an object that would otherwise be extremely difficult to study.

Building on earlier detections, the team observed LAP1-B for more than 30 hours using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They used spectroscopy, a technique that analyzes light to identify the chemical elements present in a distant object.
The observations revealed an oxygen abundance just 1/240th that of the Sun, a record low that places LAP1-B among the most chemically primitive galaxies ever characterized.

“I was instantly thrilled by the extreme lack of oxygen revealed in the data,” says Associate Professor Nakajima, the research team leader. “Finding a galaxy in such a primitive state is astonishing. It’s a chemical signature that clearly indicates a primordial galaxy caught in the moments shortly after its formation.”

The researchers also found an unusually high ratio of carbon to oxygen. That distinction matters because the relative amounts of different elements can reveal how a galaxy acquired its chemical ingredients. In LAP1-B, the elevated carbon-to-oxygen ratio closely matches theoretical predictions for material scattered into space by the explosions of the universe’s first-generation stars.
Together, these measurements suggest that LAP1-B was observed during an exceptionally early stage of chemical enrichment, when the products of the first stars were beginning to accumulate in its gas.

“Usually, we act like ‘cosmic archaeologists,’ trying to guess the past by looking at old stars in our own neighborhood. But now, we can analyze the gas directly from the original scene 13 billion years ago,” emphasizes Nakajima. “We are witnessing the moment when a galaxy first inherited the chemical building blocks created by the universe’s earliest stars.”

The galaxy’s extremely small size provides another clue about its origins. The team estimates that LAP1-B contains less than 3,300 times the Sun’s mass in stars and is associated with a halo dominated by dark matter, the invisible material thought to account for much of the mass in galaxies.

Those characteristics resemble a class of nearby objects called ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs). These exceptionally dim galaxies contain ancient stars and relatively few heavy elements, leading astronomers to suspect that they preserve conditions from the universe’s earliest periods of galaxy formation.

articles.title: NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds
articles.dek: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses.
paragraphs: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets — worlds beyond our solar system — throughout our galaxy.

“The most common source for LISA is expected to be double white dwarf systems, which are binaries composed of white dwarfs in tight orbits,” said Casey McGrath, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “If an exoplanet also orbits within one of these systems, its presence becomes imprinted on the gravitational wave signal in a way we’ll be able to uncover.”

Two papers published Tuesday in The Astrophysical Journal detail the findings. The first , authored solely by McGrath, examines the detection method and determines the planet masses and orbital periods where it would work best. The second paper , by McGrath and coauthors, investigates how such planets could be confirmed using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope .
The possibility of detecting exoplanets around LISA double white dwarf systems was first proposed by Japanese astronomer Naoki Seto in 2008.

Led by ESA (European Space Agency), the LISA mission is slated for launch in the mid-2030s. As a collaborative partner, NASA is contributing the telescopes, other critical hardware, and engineering and scientific support as part of its mission to better understand how the universe works.

The LISA detection method is similar to one called radial velocity that uses light and is already employed to find exoplanets around nearby stars. As a planet orbits, its gravity tugs on its host star, imparting a small reflex motion, or wobble, onto it. This wobble causes the star’s spectrum to oscillate, with spectral lines shifting from redder wavelengths as the star moves away from us to bluer ones as the star moves toward us. The shift is due to a phenomenon called the Doppler effect .

“Something similar occurs with gravitational waves,” said Scott Noble, a theoretical astrophysicist at NASA Goddard and a coauthor on the confirmation paper. “By themselves, double white dwarfs will emit gravitational waves at a nearly continuous frequency. Add a sufficiently massive planet to the system, and its presence causes the binary to experience reflex motion, adding a Doppler modulation to the gravitational signal.”
For LISA, this modulation will appear as sidebands, secondary signals at both higher and lower frequencies than the primary one.

McGrath likens the situation to modern radio communication, where some of the energy of a main radio carrier frequency goes into forming sidebands at adjacent upper and lower frequencies that carry messages (like voices or music). For gravitational waves, the sidebands carry messages about the presence of a planet.

White dwarfs are the Earth-sized remnants of stars like the Sun. While exoplanets have been detected around a few isolated white dwarfs, none have yet been found around a binary white dwarf, which means the LISA detections would represent a distinct new exoplanet population.

Astronomers estimate that our Milky Way galaxy contains 10 million double white dwarf systems with orbital periods of less than an hour, which generate gravitational waves in the right range for LISA to find. They expect LISA will resolve about 10,000 individual systems, as well as around 100 mixed binaries — with white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes — orbiting in similar periods.

“Once LISA captures its first exoplanet detections, it will be critical for us to validate some of them,” said Mary Anne Limbach, an assistant research scientist at the University of Michigan and a co-author on the confirmation paper. “These joint detections will allow us to establish that the gravitational signals correspond to genuine planets rather than false positives.”

The team described a new method for confirming these planets by taking advantage of the Webb telescope’s infrared sensitivity. A planet in a double white dwarf system produces a larger portion of infrared light than what’s expected from the stars themselves. Webb’s instruments can easily detect this infrared excess out to a distance of at least 500 light-years.

articles.title: Something Unusual Is Swirling around the Monster Black Hole at the Center of Our Galaxy
articles.dek: Webb’s measurements of metal-rich gas offer clues to the processes that fuel our galaxy’s supermassive black hole, which consumes material more slowly than others.
paragraphs: Webb’s measurements of metal-rich gas offer clues to the processes that fuel our galaxy’s supermassive black hole, which consumes material more slowly than others.

The gas circling the Milky Way’s central black hole is rich in metals, probably supplied by stars that exploded and released material into its surroundings over time. Researchers at McGill University’s Trottier Space Institute uncovered chemical enrichment around Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), offering clues to the origins of the material available for the black hole to consume.
For astronomers, “metals” means every element heavier than hydrogen and helium. The category includes carbon and oxygen as well as iron and gold.

Sgr A* is closer to Earth than any other supermassive black hole, making it easier to observe. The telescope measures infrared light across a wide range of wavelengths with unprecedented spectral and spatial resolution. Those capabilities allowed the researchers to distinguish the heat signatures of multiple gas clouds orbiting near the black hole and precisely measure each cloud’s metal composition.

The gas also turned out to have a composition similar to that of many stars orbiting Sgr A*. That resemblance suggests the gas and stars may have formed together. The researchers said the findings could help explain how metals are distributed around supermassive black holes in more distant galaxies, as well as the processes that supplied Earth with many of these elements.
Chemical composition also affects what happens to the gas. Metals influence how quickly it cools, which in turn influences how readily the black hole can draw it in.

“We know there’s a black hole at the center of our galaxy pulling material into itself, but we see that it’s eating a lot less material than other supermassive black holes, and more slowly,” said Nicole Ford, the study’s lead author and a PhD student in Professor Daryl Haggard’s research group in McGill’s Department of Physics. “Part of understanding why this is happening means looking at the properties of the materials available for it to consume, including gas, dust and the stars orbiting around it.”

The findings complement a recent study led by Banting Postdoctoral Fellow Mayura Balakrishnan, which examined whether the surrounding gas retained evidence of earlier bursts of energy from the black hole. That study found that local conditions shape the light emitted by the gas, making the black hole’s influence difficult to isolate. The results do not rule out past outbursts. They show that the surrounding gas cannot provide a reliable history of the black hole’s activity.
Ford said understanding how Sgr A* attracts material will require comparing these observations with simulations of how gas evolves over longer timescales.

articles.title: Scientists Discover a Strange Form of Iron on the Moon That Shouldn’t Be There
articles.dek: Scientists examining lunar soil collected by China’s Chang’e-6 mission have discovered an unexpected form of iron preserved within microscopic impact glass.
paragraphs: Scientists examining lunar soil collected by China’s Chang’e-6 mission have discovered an unexpected form of iron preserved within microscopic impact glass.

Tiny particles of iron trapped inside lunar glass may preserve evidence of the Moon’s ancient magnetic history. Scientists studying soil returned by China’s Chang’e-6 mission have identified face-centered cubic γ-Fe, an unusual form of metallic iron never before confirmed in natural lunar samples.

The discovery is particularly unexpected because γ-Fe normally exists only at high temperatures and changes into a different crystal structure as it cools. Yet researchers found that this phase of iron had survived inside microscopic glass particles formed during impacts on the lunar surface.

Researchers led by Prof. Haifeng Du of the High Magnetic Field Laboratory at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science (HFIPS) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) examined impact glass containing numerous nanoscale iron particles. Using focused ion beam preparation, transmission electron microscopy, and chemical analysis, they confirmed that γ-Fe was the dominant iron phase in the two glass samples studied. Their findings were published September 16 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) .

Under normal conditions, γ-Fe transforms into α-Fe as temperatures fall. The team proposed that the extreme conditions created by lunar impacts could prevent this transformation. Rapid cooling of molten material, small amounts of carbon and other elements, and the surrounding glassy matrix may have helped preserve the unusual crystal structure at the lunar surface.

The scientists also investigated whether these particles could retain magnetic information. Using off-axis electron holography, a technique that can map magnetic fields at extremely small scales, they examined the magnetic structure of individual γ-Fe nanoparticles. Relatively large particles displayed a stable single-vortex magnetic state, with their magnetization arranged in a circulating pattern. They also maintained a stable magnetic response when exposed to an external magnetic field.
“This tiny magnetic fossil may help us better understand the Moon’s ancient magnetic history,” said Dr. Long Li of HFIPS, a member of the research team.

Although the Moon no longer possesses a global magnetic field, its rocks and soils contain magnetic minerals that can preserve information about past conditions. The newly identified γ-Fe expands the range of materials scientists can investigate when reconstructing that history.

Because γ-Fe and α-Fe develop under different physical conditions and exhibit distinct magnetic properties, they may retain records from different stages of lunar impact events. Further research will be needed to determine how reliably these minerals preserve ancient magnetic signals and what they can reveal about the evolution of magnetism on the Moon.

articles.title: US national debt keeps rising after years of tax cuts – and this will make policymaking all the more difficult
articles.dek: Democrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the…
paragraphs: Democrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U. S. economy.

Clocking in at US$32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living .

Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes . Even as the U. S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt.

The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found.

The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar , I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact . But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper , the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts.
I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing.
Proponents of fiscal austerity argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise.
U. S. federal spending, however, has remained relatively flat – outside of emergencies like the 2009 recovery package and COVID-19 stimulus funds – even as GDP has risen.

At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a study by the Tax Foundation , a nonpartisan think tank, noted.

President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2. 9% of GDP, according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis . The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1. 8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth.
Coming in sixth place at 1. 2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts.

While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91. 2% to 97. 1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall 10-year cost of $1. 5 trillion . That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025.

But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through Trump’s legislation that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts.

The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would add another $3. 4 trillion over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to 116% of GDP by the end of 2034 .
A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not.

If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, debt remains stable . The problem for the U. S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while interest payments on government debt are rising as well.

This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U. S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with lower tax revenue due to tax cuts , the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office.

In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U. S. took in more tax revenue than it spent and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats.

It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U. S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century.
